title: Forward pass, loss and gradient descent in one dimension

videos.script: In lesson 1, every weight was written by hand, and nobody trains a network that way. {{hand}} This lesson lets a program find a weight on its own, using the smallest model there is. {{model}} It has one input and one weight, and its prediction is their product, fitted to ten points. {{points}} Computing that prediction is the forward pass. At the slope the points were made with, it misses all ten. {{forward}} The loss turns ten errors into one number: square each error, then take the mean. {{loss}} Try a few weights and the loss draws a valley, with the best weight at the bottom. {{valley}} At any point, the slope of that valley says which way is down. {{slope}} Gradient descent takes a step against the slope, then does it again. After eight steps the weight stops moving. {{steps}} How far each step goes is the learning rate. Too small, and it crawls towards the bottom. Too large, and it overshoots, then flies off. {{rates}} Give the model a second parameter, and the valley becomes a surface. The slope becomes an arrow with two parts, called the gradient. {{bowl}} Every network in this course learns this way, with thousands of parameters instead of one. {{end}}
